Felix’s voice broke the silence, flat and quiet. “You would have been brought back.” David looked up at that — mouth parting, maybe to protest, maybe to argue. Felix didn’t let him, raising a hand to cut off his reply. “But not all of you.” The words were precise . Surgical in their restraint. Carefully chosen. David stared at him. Felix’s eyes didn’t meet his this time. They drifted toward the fire — like whatever he was about to say was easier to aim at the flames. “You know what happens,” he said. “They come back, sure. But they don’t always remember. They forget names. Details. Whole people .” His voice didn’t shake. But something in it cracked — as if it had to be said before it turned to ash in his throat. “I’ve watched it happen,” Felix said, his voice softer now. Thinner. “I’ve watched someone stare straight through their own teammate like they were a stranger. Because the Fog took that thread from them. And it never came back.” David swallowed. Hard. His throat felt tight, raw — The words somehow lodging there instead of landing clean. Felix looked at him then. Really looked. Not through the fire. Not past him. At him. His eyes were sharp, but there was something exposed there too — something he wasn’t used to letting show. “If you’d died today,” he said quietly, “And I had to sit across from you tomorrow while you acted like we’d never even met—” He stopped. Didn’t finish. Didn’t need to. The thought hung there, complete on its own. David felt the burn settle low in his gut. This had never been about the injury at all. This had been about loss for Felix. Not the kind that the survivors were used to — bleeding, screaming, that moment of panic before getting brought back — but the kind that erases . There was a sudden pressure behind David’s ribs — something inside that had cracked open and didn’t know how to close again. Too wide. Too raw. A guilt that filled every available space. His hands moved without aim — one pressing instinctively to his injured arm, the other twisting in his lap like it was trying to find something to hold on to. He fixed his gaze on the fire again, too uncomfortable to keep facing Felix. The man’s anger at him had hurt before, sure, but now it hurt in a way that mattered . He didn’t know what to do with that. His voice came out small and bare. Fragile in a way none of them were used to hearing from him. “I figured... worst case, I’d reset. Take the hit. Come back fresh.” He swallowed, the firelight highlighting the shame that flushed up the sides of his neck. “I didn’t think anyone would—” He stopped himself. Breathed. Tried again. “I didn’t mean to scare you.” It wasn’t eloquent. Wasn’t grand. But at least it was honest, even if it hurt just to say it. David finally glanced up — a flick of the eyes, barely enough to register, but full of a silent, desperate wish that something in Felix’s expression would have softened by now. That this could be over. That the worst had already passed. He wasn't that lucky. Felix’s face hadn’t changed. There was no rage. No heat. Just the weight of disappointment. And that was somehow worse. “You didn’t just scare me,” His voice calm, matter of fact, “You almost erased yourself. ” David, who had thrown himself in front of killers, taken hits without flinching, bled out beneath hooks and crawlspaces and basement stairs — who thought he knew what damage felt like — had no armor for that. He gaze wilted back down into the fire. And for the first time since they’d pulled him out of the rubble, he felt like maybe he hadn’t actually made it out at all. The silence that followed could’ve been carved with a knife. Even the fire seemed to crackle more quietly now—its usual hisses and pops reduced to something hesitant, like it was trying not to intrude. David looked ready to dissolve into the stone beneath him. Felix was still watching, still unreadable — eyes narrowed, posture tight, like he hadn’t decided if this counted as closure or just damage control. CRACK The fire split open with a sudden snap as a log shifted. The sound rang longer than it should have, snapping through the quiet like a warning shot. Dwight jumped so hard he nearly dropped the marshmallow stick he hadn’t actually used in the last twenty minutes. It clattered against the stone, and he fumbled to pick it up like it mattered. Jill, who had been studiously examining a patch of gravel like it held the secrets to the universe, finally cleared her throat. “Well,” she said lightly, a forced cheer pushing through the awkward tension, “remind me never to leave you boys unsupervised again.” Felix blinked and startled slightly, like he’d forgotten anyone else was there. David exhaled, shoulders slumping. Tension bleeding out like someone had finally released the pressure valve around his lungs. “You miss all the fun, Jill,” Dwight muttered, forcing a grin. “You chose to run Nemesis around for half the trial.” “Well, someone needed to.” Jill tossed a pebble at his boot. “If I’d known you were gonna start a landslide while I was out playing fetch with Frankenstein, I’d have brought snacks.” Felix let out a quiet huff. Possibly a laugh. Possibly a sound of exhausted despair. Hard to say. David just scrubbed both hands over his face, like he wanted to erase the last ten minutes from existence by sheer force of will.
